Let's keep this going. Part of the problem is that the compass analogy assumes that one needs to have an orientation (true north) and an azimuth. That you have a direction. Whereas wandering through a thicket one loses the pebbles in the undergrowth. Getting lost may, in fact, be the point. Or perhaps an unavoidable outcome.

Maybe the appropriate analogy is Ingold's Wayfaring.

In Lines, Tim Ingold separates navigation, point to point across a pre-mapped surface, from wayfaring: knowing as you go, the path made by walking it. He also sets the network of connected points against the meshwork of entangled lines. A thicket is a meshwork, which fits Venkat's "not a graph" intuition better than the maze. Design for wayfaring looks different:

Trails, not pebbles. Leave a line, not points: footprints, not signposts. The record of the wander is the artifact, as in Vannevar Bush's Memex, where the shared trail was the unit of value.
Trails fade unless re-walked. Desire paths wear in with use and grow over without it. No map, just worn ways. The scene is where trails cross.
Landmarks, not headings. Kevin Lynch, in The Image of the City, argues that people orient by landmarks, not coordinates. Here the landmarks are precedents: heavily quoted, heavily forked items glimpsed through the trees.
Etak. Keep the canoe still and let the islands move. The UI shows how landmarks have shifted around you.
Be found. Ask "what finds me while I'm lost?" A landmark, a crossing trail, an old trail someone just re-walked.
The protocol-native version: a trail is itself a blyg item, quotes and glosses published as you walk, forkable, with lineage for free. Reading becomes writing. That's a better reply to Venkat than any mockup.

The thicket is a maze-like oriented space, not a graph

A strong suspicion i have is that the RSS/feed style blyg reading might be the wrong UI. I think it needs something more geographic but I can't even think of what to ask the AI to build. Maps and terrains, and pixel art like interactions all feel wrong.

I agree

Current is a cool attempt at an ephemeral RSS reader that I enjoy because it doesn't feel like an inbox / homework. However, the time-sequential feed feels less appropriate for people whose interests wander widely then return to prior thoughts.
